summary:
The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islanders, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the male-sex offences from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent explicitly not a defence. Reported maximum terms differ across sources: the 2017 coverage gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to ten years for indecent acts between males. All sources agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited. The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage is not recognised locally and a trans visitor in a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing.
tangentialFactors:
The repeal followed a protracted legislative path. A 2017 select committee recommended removing sections 154 and 155, and the provisions were struck from the draft Crimes Bill, drafted with New Zealand assistance; MPs subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 members again pushed the bill's report back, this time by three months, before the 2023 passage.

Reporting on the 2020 deferral attributes the taboo underlying sections 154 and 155 to colonisation, describing the society as historically accepting of same-sex relations before that period.

Public submissions on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill opened in Parliament on 10 August 2017, the bill being intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act.
localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association, the country's only LGBTI community group, appeared before the select committee and welcomed the draft reform; a member publicly described the 1969 provisions as homophobic. At least three lawyers were expected to speak to the committee on penalties and sentencing.

The 1969 offences were never enforced against residents in living memory, so there is no record of prosecutions of local men under sections 154 and 155.

The marriage bar applies to residents as well as visitors: Cook Islanders cannot contract a same-sex marriage locally, and no local mechanism recognises one contracted abroad.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty figures for the 1969 provisions remain unresolved across the sources: the 2017 coverage gives seven years and five years, and the 2023 repeal coverage gives up to ten years. The inventory does not settle which figures were correct in the statute as it stood before 1 June 2023.

No source in the inventory addresses gender-marker change on birth certificates or passports, entry or security screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, or whether a New Zealand passport bearing a trans marker is accepted without question at Cook Islands entry.

Also unsourced: any anti-discrimination protection expressly covering gender identity, hate-crime provisions that would aggravate an attack on a trans person, facility or restroom access rules, and access to gender-affirming healthcare or to continued hormone treatment on the islands.

The inventory contains no reporting of violence against trans people in the Cook Islands, and no official statement from the Cook Islands government or the New Zealand government on trans-specific protection or risk.
